claim: D. melanogaster Cdt1 has an N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predicted by DISOPRED.
source: Sequence analysis with the disorder prediction server DISOPRED (Jones and Cozzetto, 2015) reveals that the N-terminal sequence of DmCdt1 is predicted to be an extended intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational prediction using DISOPRED and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An N-terminal IDR is present in other metazoan Cdt1s.
source: Although the sequence of this region is not conserved per se, an N-terminal IDR is present in other metazoan Cdt1s (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing IDR presence across metazoan species.

claim: DmCdt1 binds to DNA-coupled agarose beads.
source: DmCdt1 but not ScCdt1 bound to the DNA-coupled beads.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B using DNA pulldown assays.

claim: ScCdt1 does not bind to DNA-coupled agarose beads.
source: DmCdt1 but not ScCdt1 bound to the DNA-coupled beads.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B using DNA pulldown assays.

claim: ScCdt1 showed no evidence of DNA binding in fluorescence anisotropy measurements.
source: ScCdt1 showed no evidence of binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DmCdt1 binds DNA with a Kd,app of 83 ± 17 nM.
source: DmCdt1 bound with a Kd, app = 83 ± 17 nM.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The complex between DNA and DmCdt1 is heterogeneous and large.
source: The complex between DNA and DmCdt1 is heterogeneous and large, and is fully well-shifted at the highest concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The calculated Kd,app for DmCdt1 DNA binding is approximately 100 nM by EMSA.
source: In good agreement with anisotropy measurements, the calculated Kd, app for DmCdt1 is ~100 nM.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1D and is consistent with fluorescence anisotropy measurements.

claim: Mixing concentrated DmCdt1 with duplex DNA results in a visible increase in solution turbidity.
source: Mixing concentrated DmCdt1 with duplex DNA results in a visible increase in solution turbidity that can be reversed with the addition of KCl.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The turbidity caused by mixing DmCdt1 with DNA can be reversed with the addition of KCl.
source: Mixing concentrated DmCdt1 with duplex DNA results in a visible increase in solution turbidity that can be reversed with the addition of KCl.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Phase-separated droplets are evident when Cdt1 is mixed with DNA.
source: Phase-separated droplets were evident when Cdt1 was mixed with DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by DIC microscopy analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Purified DmCdt1 is monodisperse in solution as assessed by analytical size-exclusion chromatography.
source: size-exclusion chromatography showed that purified DmCdt1 is monodisperse in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cdt1 phase separation is observed with oligonucleotides longer than 25 basepairs.
source: Cdt1 phase separation is observed with oligonucleotides longer than 25 basepairs.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cdt1 phase separation depends on the length but not the sequence of the dsDNA substrate.
source: Notably, Cdt1 phase separation was dependent on the length, but not the sequence, of the dsDNA substrate, with maximal LLPS occurring in the presence of oligonucleotides longer than 25 basepairs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Randomly generated 60 bp oligonucleotides containing between 10–75% GC content are equally potent at inducing Cdt1 phase separation.
source: All are equally potent.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Unlabeled dsDNA can effectively compete with the DNA of a preformed Cdt1/Cy5-dsDNA complex with Kc,app = 64 nM.
source: Unlabeled dsDNA is able to effectively compete with the DNA of a preformed Cdt1/Cy5-dsDNA complex (Kc, app = 64 nM, a value comparable to the observed Kd, app for DNA binding of 83 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization competition assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Kc,app value of 64 nM is comparable to the observed Kd,app for DNA binding of 83 nM.
source: Unlabeled dsDNA is able to effectively compete with the DNA of a preformed Cdt1/Cy5-dsDNA complex (Kc, app = 64 nM, a value comparable to the observed Kd, app for DNA binding of 83 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of competition and binding assay data.

claim: The labeled DNA in Cdt1 droplets is freely exchangeable and in equilibrium between bound and unbound states.
source: The unlabeled oligonucleotide was able to fully reduce DNA binding by Cdt1 to background levels, with an inhibition constant (Kc, app = 62 ± 4 nM) comparable to the observed Kd, app (83 nM), demonstrating that the labeled DNA in droplets is freely exchangeable and therefore in equilibrium between bound and unbound states.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data demonstrating reversible binding.

claim: DmCdt1 binds DNA and DNA-binding induces the protein to phase separate.
source: Together, these data demonstrate not only that DmCdt1 binds DNA, but that DNA-binding in turn induces the protein to phase separate.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including pulldown, fluorescence anisotropy, EMSA, and microscopy.

claim: When eGFP-Cdt1 was mixed with Cy5-dsDNA, droplets up to 3 µm in diameter appeared containing both protein and nucleic acid.
source: When eGFP-Cdt1 was mixed with Cy5-dsDNA, droplets up to 3 µm in diameter appeared, all containing both protein and nucleic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by two-color fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Samples with eGFP-Cdt1 alone did not show droplets.
source: Samples with eGFP-Cdt1 alone did not show such droplets, nor were they observed for samples with Cy5-dsDNA only.
evidence: The claim is supported by two-color fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Samples with Cy5-dsDNA only did not show droplets.
source: Samples with eGFP-Cdt1 alone did not show such droplets, nor were they observed for samples with Cy5-dsDNA only.
evidence: The claim is supported by two-color fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Phase separation by Cdt1 is driven, at least in part, by dsDNA-induced coacervation.
source: These data demonstrate that phase separation by Cdt1 is driven, at least in part, by dsDNA-induced coacervation, and further show that dye-labeled oligonucleotides can serve as a proxy for labeled protein when assessing DNA-dependent protein phase separation by fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: The claim is supported by two-color fluorescence imaging data showing co-localization of protein and DNA in droplets.

claim: Dye-labeled oligonucleotides can serve as a proxy for labeled protein when assessing DNA-dependent protein phase separation by fluorescence microscopy.
source: These data demonstrate that phase separation by Cdt1 is driven, at least in part, by dsDNA-induced coacervation, and further show that dye-labeled oligonucleotides can serve as a proxy for labeled protein when assessing DNA-dependent protein phase separation by fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations showing that labeled DNA can be used to visualize droplets.

claim: Only wild-type Cdt1 could induce droplet formation, not Cdt1ΔIDR.
source: Only WT Cdt1 could induce droplet formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C comparing WT and ΔIDR constructs.

claim: No depletion of full-length Cdt1 was observed in the absence of DNA.
source: In agreement with the microscopy data, no depletion of full-length Cdt1 was observed relative to the load control in the absence of DNA (Figure 2E), indicating that no phase separation occurred.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Full-length Cdt1 signal was fully lost from the supernatant in the presence of DNA.
source: Moreover, the full-length Cdt1 signal was fully lost from the supernatant in the presence of DNA, indicating that a near complete partitioning of Cdt1 into the condensed (pelleted) phase took place.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: When the DmCdt1 IDR was removed, the protein was fully retained in the supernatant, regardless of whether DNA was present or not.
source: When the DmCdt1 IDR was removed, the protein was again fully retained in the supernatant, regardless of whether DNA was present or not.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The Cdt1 N-terminal IDR alone (Cdt1IDR) bound DNA with Kd,app = 158 ± 32 nM.
source: Notably, a construct containing only the Cdt1 N-terminal IDR residues (Cdt1IDR) bound DNA (Kd, app = 158 ± 32 nM) and underwent DNA-dependent phase separation on its own (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), demonstrating that the Cdt1 IDR is necessary and sufficient for condensation and that it directly interacts with dsDNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Cdt1 IDR is necessary and sufficient for condensation.
source: Notably, a construct containing only the Cdt1 N-terminal IDR residues (Cdt1IDR) bound DNA (Kd, app = 158 ± 32 nM) and underwent DNA-dependent phase separation on its own (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), demonstrating that the Cdt1 IDR is necessary and sufficient for condensation and that it directly interacts with dsDNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that the IDR alone can bind DNA and phase separate.

claim: The Cdt1 IDR directly interacts with dsDNA.
source: Notably, a construct containing only the Cdt1 N-terminal IDR residues (Cdt1IDR) bound DNA (Kd, app = 158 ± 32 nM) and underwent DNA-dependent phase separation on its own (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), demonstrating that the Cdt1 IDR is necessary and sufficient for condensation and that it directly interacts with dsDNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA binding and phase separation data for the isolated IDR.

claim: Budding yeast Cdt1 does not exhibit phase separation behavior in vitro.
source: Budding yeast Cdt1, which neither has an IDR (Table 1) nor binds DNA (Figure 1), did not exhibit phase separation behavior in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay and microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: All metazoan Cdt1 homologs possess an N-terminal IDR.
source: However, all other metazoan Cdt1 homologs possess an N-terminal IDR; tests with human Cdt1 revealed that, similar to DmCdt1, it also can undergo DNA-induced liquid phase condensation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Human Cdt1 can undergo DNA-induced liquid phase condensation.
source: However, all other metazoan Cdt1 homologs possess an N-terminal IDR; tests with human Cdt1 revealed that, similar to DmCdt1, it also can undergo DNA-induced liquid phase condensation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay and microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Metazoan Cdt1 IDRs are essential for DNA-promoted phase separation.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate the essential role of metazoan Cdt1 IDRs in facilitating DNA-promoted phase separation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing that IDR deletion abolishes phase separation.

claim: During active replication in the early D. melanogaster embryo (0–2 hr), Cdt1 concentration peaks at approximately 70 nM.
source: During active replication in the early D. melanogaster embryo (0–2 hr), Cdt1 concentration peaks at approximately 70 nM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot quantitation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: Droplets were observed down to the lowest concentration of Cdt1 tested (62.5 nM) when salt concentrations were at or below physiological levels ([KGlutamate]=150 mM).
source: Droplets were observed down to the lowest concentration of Cdt1 tested (62.5 nM) when salt concentrations were set at or below physiological levels ([KGlutamate]=150 mM).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase diagram data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Increasing salt concentration to twice physiological levels (300 mM) shifted the concentration of protein necessary to see phase separation to 500 nM.
source: Increasing salt concentration to twice physiological levels (300 mM) shifted the concentration of protein necessary to see phase separation to 500 nM.
evidence: The claim is supported by phase diagram data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: When the concentration of potassium glutamate was increased to 600 mM, no phase separation was observed for any concentration of Cdt1 tested.
source: When the concentration of potassium glutamate was increased to 600 mM, no phase separation was observed for any concentration of Cdt1 tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by phase diagram data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: DNA-coupled loss of Cdt1 signal was seen at all concentrations tested (800 nM to 50 nM).
source: DNA-coupled loss of Cdt1 signal was seen at all concentrations tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: DmCdt1 undergoes DNA-dependent phase separation at physiological protein and salt concentrations.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that DmCdt1 undergoes DNA-dependent phase separation at physiological protein and salt concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by phase diagram and depletion assay data at nanomolar protein concentrations.

claim: Cdc6 and two subunits of ORC (Orc1 and Orc2) possess a high level of disordered content as a proportion of their total polypeptide chain length.
source: In addition to Cdt1, Cdc6 and two subunits of ORC (Orc1 and Orc2) were found to possess a high level of disordered content as a proportion of their total polypeptide chain length, and each contained a continuous region of disorder longer than 200 amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by DISOPRED analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Orc1, Orc2, and Cdc6 each contain a continuous region of disorder longer than 200 amino acids.
source: In addition to Cdt1, Cdc6 and two subunits of ORC (Orc1 and Orc2) were found to possess a high level of disordered content as a proportion of their total polypeptide chain length, and each contained a continuous region of disorder longer than 200 amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by DISOPRED analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Mcm2-7 subunits contain less than 30% predicted disordered sequence overall.
source: Conversely, the Mcm2-7 subunits, though possessing unstructured regions, contain less than 30% predicted disordered sequence overall, with no single disordered region extending beyond 150 amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by DISOPRED analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No single disordered region in Mcm2-7 subunits extends beyond 150 amino acids.
source: Conversely, the Mcm2-7 subunits, though possessing unstructured regions, contain less than 30% predicted disordered sequence overall, with no single disordered region extending beyond 150 amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by DISOPRED analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ORC phase separates in a DNA-dependent fashion in the presence and absence of ATP.
source: ORC (500 nM) phase separates in a DNA-dependent fashion in the presence and absence of ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the presence of ORC, large phase-separated droplets formed with Cy5-dsDNA.
source: In the presence of ORC, large phase-separated droplets formed.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Orc1 IDR is longer than the Orc2 IDR by approximately 100 residues.
source: In terms of length, the Orc1 IDR, at 362 amino acids, is approximately 100 residues longer than the Orc2 IDR (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The IDRs of Orc1 and Orc2 are highly similar in amino acid composition.
source: Comparisons of sequence composition between Orc1 and Orc2 IDRs – performed by calculating the relative percentage of hydrophobic (A, G, I, L, M, P, V), hydrophilic (C, N, S, T, Q), charged (D, E, H, K, R), and aromatic (F, W, Y) residues – show that the IDRs of Orc1 and Orc2 are highly similar in content, with the values for Orc1 and Orc2 within 3% for each amino acid category.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence composition analysis.

claim: Orc1 and Orc2 IDR amino acids are near equally distributed across hydrophobic (36/35%), hydrophilic (30/29%), and charged (32/33%) classes.
source: Interestingly, Orc1 and Orc2 IDR amino acids are near equally distributed across hydrophobic (36/35%), hydrophilic (30/29%), and charged (32/33%) classes; this preponderance of hydrophobic residues is somewhat unexpected given the predicted unstructured nature of these sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence composition analysis.

claim: The Orc1 IDR (pI = 10.1) is enriched for positively-charged residues (20% positive and 12% negative).
source: Although the Orc1 and Orc2 IDRs are highly similar in terms of amino acid types, they do show a marked difference in their isoelectric points (pI): the Orc1 IDR (pI = 10.1) is enriched for positively-charged residues (20% positive and 12% negative), whereas the Orc2 IDR (pI = 6.0) is weakly enriched for negatively-charged residues (17% negative and 16% positive).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: The Orc2 IDR (pI = 6.0) is weakly enriched for negatively-charged residues (17% negative and 16% positive).
source: Although the Orc1 and Orc2 IDRs are highly similar in terms of amino acid types, they do show a marked difference in their isoelectric points (pI): the Orc1 IDR (pI = 10.1) is enriched for positively-charged residues (20% positive and 12% negative), whereas the Orc2 IDR (pI = 6.0) is weakly enriched for negatively-charged residues (17% negative and 16% positive).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: Loss of the Orc1 IDR abolishes phase separation.
source: Loss of the Orc1 IDR abolishes phase separation but loss of the Orc2 IDR has no effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Loss of the Orc2 IDR has no effect on phase separation.
source: Loss of the Orc1 IDR abolishes phase separation but loss of the Orc2 IDR has no effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ORC1ΔIDR showed no evidence for phase separation.
source: ORC1ΔIDR showed no evidence for phase separation in either assay, whereas the construct lacking the Orc2 IDR exhibited wild-type behavior in both assays (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay and microscopy data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The construct lacking the Orc2 IDR exhibited wild-type behavior in phase separation assays.
source: ORC1ΔIDR showed no evidence for phase separation in either assay, whereas the construct lacking the Orc2 IDR exhibited wild-type behavior in both assays (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay and microscopy data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Drosophila ORC phase separates using interactions that require the N-terminal IDR of Orc1 but not Orc2.
source: These findings demonstrate that Drosophila ORC phase separates using interactions that require the N-terminal IDR of Orc1 but not Orc2.
evidence: The claim is supported by deletion analysis showing differential requirements for Orc1 and Orc2 IDRs.

claim: The Orc1 IDR is relatively well-conserved across the Drosophila genus (67% identity).
source: Given the predicted lack of structure in the Orc1 IDR we were surprised to discover that this region is relatively well-conserved across the Drosophila genus (67% identity, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and that the composition, length, and pI of this region is conserved across the metazoan phyla (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The composition, length, and pI of the Orc1 IDR is conserved across the metazoan phyla.
source: Given the predicted lack of structure in the Orc1 IDR we were surprised to discover that this region is relatively well-conserved across the Drosophila genus (67% identity, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and that the composition, length, and pI of this region is conserved across the metazoan phyla (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: S. cerevisiae Orc1 possesses an N-terminal IDR that is shorter than observed in metazoa and has an acidic pI.
source: Although S. cerevisiae Orc1 possesses an N-terminal IDR, this region is shorter than observed in metazoa and also has an acidic pI (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Budding yeast ORC does not phase separate.
source: Consistent with this observation, budding yeast ORC does not phase separate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DmCdc6 interacts with DNA by dsDNA-coupled agarose bead pull-down assays.
source: Similar to budding yeast Cdc6 (Feng et al., 2000), DmCdc6 was found to interact with DNA by dsDNA-coupled agarose bead pull-down assays; the presence of ATP had no significant effect on Cdc6 DNA-binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The presence of ATP had no significant effect on Cdc6 DNA-binding.
source: Similar to budding yeast Cdc6 (Feng et al., 2000), DmCdc6 was found to interact with DNA by dsDNA-coupled agarose bead pull-down assays; the presence of ATP had no significant effect on Cdc6 DNA-binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A reproducible DNA-dependent depletion of Cdc6 from the supernatant was observed.
source: Upon testing whether Cdc6 phase separates in the presence of DNA using the depletion assay (Figure 3G), we observed a reproducible DNA-dependent depletion of Cdc6 from the supernatant (Figure 3G lanes 1–3); however, in contrast to ORC, this depletion was inhibited by the presence of ATP (Figure 3G lanes 4–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Cdc6 depletion was inhibited by the presence of ATP.
source: Upon testing whether Cdc6 phase separates in the presence of DNA using the depletion assay (Figure 3G), we observed a reproducible DNA-dependent depletion of Cdc6 from the supernatant (Figure 3G lanes 1–3); however, in contrast to ORC, this depletion was inhibited by the presence of ATP (Figure 3G lanes 4–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ATP can function as a hydrotrope to enhance intracellular protein solubility.
source: A recent report that ATP can function as a hydrotrope to enhance intracellular protein solubility may provide an explanation for its effect on Cdc6 phase separation (Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cdc6 was only partially depleted from the supernatant at higher concentrations, unlike DmCdt1 which fully partitioned into phases.
source: Repeating the assay at higher concentrations of DmCdc6 shows that unlike DmCdt1, which appeared to fully partition into phases at higher concentrations (Figure 2E), Cdc6 was only partially depleted from the supernatant (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Cdc6 underwent complete partitioning into the condensed phase in the presence of plasmid DNA.
source: Notably, Cdc6 underwent complete partitioning into the condensed phase in the presence of plasmid DNA, whereas only partial depletion was observed with short oligonucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), indicating that for DmCdc6, LLPS requires longer DNA segments than either DmCdt1 or DmORC.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: For DmCdc6, LLPS requires longer DNA segments than either DmCdt1 or DmORC.
source: Notably, Cdc6 underwent complete partitioning into the condensed phase in the presence of plasmid DNA, whereas only partial depletion was observed with short oligonucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), indicating that for DmCdc6, LLPS requires longer DNA segments than either DmCdt1 or DmORC.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of depletion assay data with different DNA lengths.

claim: Fluorescence microscopy confirmed that Cdc6 forms condensates.
source: Fluorescence microscopy with Cy5-dsDNA confirmed that Cdc6 forms condensates in these conditions (Figure 3I), while tests with a Cdc6 mutant lacking the N-terminal IDR (Cdc6ΔIDR) (Figure 3J) showed that this construct has no capacity to phase separate (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Cdc6ΔIDR has no capacity to phase separate.
source: Fluorescence microscopy with Cy5-dsDNA confirmed that Cdc6 forms condensates in these conditions (Figure 3I), while tests with a Cdc6 mutant lacking the N-terminal IDR (Cdc6ΔIDR) (Figure 3J) showed that this construct has no capacity to phase separate (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay and microscopy data shown in Figure 3J-K.

claim: Drosophila Cdc6 can form DNA-dependent condensates in a manner that requires its N-terminal IDR.
source: Collectively, these studies confirm that Drosophila Cdc6 can form DNA-dependent condensates in a manner that requires its N-terminal IDR.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing DNA-dependent phase separation that is abolished by IDR deletion.

claim: Both tRFP-Cdc6 and eGFP-Cdt1 showed marked enrichment within ORC droplets.
source: Both tRFP-Cdc6 and eGFP-Cdt1 showed marked enrichment within ORC droplets (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All three initiator components can co-associate in a liquid phase in the presence of ATP.
source: Moreover, although phase separation by Cdc6 was partially inhibited by ATP, all three initiator components can co-associate in a liquid phase in the presence of ATP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The presence of other initiators overcomes the ATP barrier to Cdc6 phase separation and allows the full suite of helicase loading factors to co-localize into a highly concentrated protein/nucleic acid-rich phase.
source: Thus, while ATP appears to impede phase separation by Cdc6 on its own, the presence of the other initiators overcomes this barrier and allows the full suite of helicase loading factors to co-localize into a highly concentrated protein/nucleic acid-rich phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing co-localization of all initiators in the presence of ATP.

claim: In samples containing eGFP-Cdt1, all ORC/Cy5-dsDNA droplets are enriched for eGFP signal.
source: In samples containing eGFP-Cdt1, all ORC/Cy5-dsDNA droplets are enriched for eGFP signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No enrichment of eGFP-FUS is observed in ORC/Cy5-dsDNA droplets.
source: No enrichment is observed in samples containing eGFP-FUS.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A 10-fold enrichment of eGFP-Cdt1 signal intensity is observed within ORC/Cy5-dsdNA droplets relative to the bulk phase.
source: Relative to the bulk phase, a 10-fold enrichment of eGFP-Cdt1 signal intensity is observed within ORC/Cy5-dsdNA droplets (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Initiator condensates show a degree of specificity that allows for exclusion of other proteins with non-congruent IDRs.
source: Thus, initiator condensates show a degree of specificity that allows for exclusion of other proteins with non-congruent IDRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing selective recruitment of Cdt1 but not FUS into ORC droplets.

claim: No evidence for phase separation by Mcm2-7 alone was observed in the presence or absence of ATP.
source: No evidence for phase separation by Mcm2-7 alone was observed under these conditions either in the presence or absence of ATP (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The IDRs of Mcm2 and Mcm3 have an acidic pI (pI <6).
source: The IDRs of Mcm2 and Mcm3, for example, have an acidic pI (pI <6), and although Mcm4 contains an N-terminal IDR with a basic pI (pI = 11.0), this region has fewer charged residues compared to the other initiator IDRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mcm4 contains an N-terminal IDR with a basic pI (pI = 11.0) but this region has fewer charged residues compared to the other initiator IDRs.
source: The IDRs of Mcm2 and Mcm3, for example, have an acidic pI (pI <6), and although Mcm4 contains an N-terminal IDR with a basic pI (pI = 11.0), this region has fewer charged residues compared to the other initiator IDRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fluorescence microscopy with FLAG-Mcm2-7 and Cy5-dsDNA showed no evidence of droplet formation.
source: Fluorescence microscopy with FLAG-Mcm2-7 and Cy5-dsDNA showed no evidence of droplet formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), confirming that Mcm2-7 does not undergo phase separation.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mcm2-7 recruitment to and stable loading on DNA requires the formation of a pre-Replicative Complex (pre-RC) containing ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1.
source: Mcm2-7 recruitment to and stable loading on DNA requires the formation of a pre-Replicative Complex (pre-RC) containing ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1 (Bowers et al., 2004; Evrin et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: No appreciable pelleting of Mcm2-7 alone was observed in the presence or absence of ATP, or with just the OCC.
source: No appreciable pelleting of Mcm2-7 alone was observed in either the presence or absence of ATP, or with just the OCC; however, when ATP was included with the OCC, an ~8 fold enrichment of Mcm2-7 was observed in the pelleted phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: When ATP was included with the OCC, an ~8 fold enrichment of Mcm2-7 was observed in the pelleted phase.
source: No appreciable pelleting of Mcm2-7 alone was observed in either the presence or absence of ATP, or with just the OCC; however, when ATP was included with the OCC, an ~8 fold enrichment of Mcm2-7 was observed in the pelleted phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: DmMcm2-7 does not phase separate on its own, but can be specifically recruited into condensates when initiation factors and ATP are present.
source: These data demonstrate that although DmMcm2-7 does not phase separate on its own, it can be specifically recruited into condensates when initiation factors and ATP are present.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data showing selective recruitment under specific conditions.

claim: No enrichment of Mcm2-7 in the condensed phase is observed when any one of the initiation proteins (ORC, Cdc6, or Cdt1) is omitted from the reaction.
source: Whereas partitioning of Mcm2-7 into the condensed phase is seen with the intact OCC, no enrichment of the helicase complex is observed when any one of the initiation proteins is omitted from the reaction (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Mcm2-7 does not phase separate on its own, but can be selectively enriched in condensed phases containing all of the factors required for helicase loading (ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1) and ATP.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that Mcm2-7 does not phase separate on its own, but that it can be selectively enriched in condensed phases containing all of the factors required for helicase loading (ORC, Cdc6, and Cdt1) and ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple depletion assays showing requirements for recruitment.

claim: Initiator IDRs have a distinct amino acid sequence signature compared to other phase-separating factors such as human FUS and EWS, or C. elegans Laf1.
source: Initiator IDRs have a distinct amino acid sequence signature compared to other phase-separating factors such as human FUS and EWS, or C. elegans Laf1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence composition analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Initiator IDRs can be characterized as having: 1) a high degree of sequence complexity, and approximately equal representation of charged, hydrophilic, and hydrophobic residues, 2) a deficiency in aromatic amino acids and glycine, and 3) a net positive charge.
source: Generally speaking, initiator IDRs can be characterized as having: 1) a high degree of sequence complexity, and approximately equal representation of charged, hydrophilic, and hydrophobic residues, 2) a deficiency in aromatic amino acids and glycine, and 3) a net positive charge.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence composition analysis.

claim: The tight binding of DNA by yeast and metazoan ORC is dependent upon ATP binding to its Orc1 subunit.
source: However, previous work has demonstrated that the tight binding of DNA by yeast and metazoan ORC is dependent upon ATP binding to its Orc1 subunit (Bell and Stillman, 1992; Bleichert et al., 2018; Chesnokov et al., 2001; Giordano-Coltart et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A discrete patch within the DmOrc1 IDR that is close to the protein's ATPase domain has been demonstrated as necessary but not sufficient for the ATP-dependent binding of DNA by ORC in vitro.
source: A discrete patch within the DmOrc1 IDR that is close to the protein's ATPase domain has been demonstrated as necessary but not sufficient for the ATP-dependent binding of DNA by ORC in vitro (Bleichert et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A transgenic fly line expressing eGFP-tagged Orc1 under the control of its endogenous promoter can rescue a null allele.
source: A transgenic fly line expressing eGFP-tagged Orc1 under the control of its endogenous promoter was made, and the functional integrity of this transgene confirmed by its ability to rescue a null allele (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Table 2.

claim: eGFP-Orc1WalkerAB was unable to rescue the null allele.
source: Genetic crosses revealed that eGFP-Orc1WalkerAB was unable to rescue the null allele (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Table 2.

claim: ORC associates with anaphase chromosomes in the early D. melanogaster embryo.
source: Previous work with a transgenic fly line expressing an eGFP-tagged Orc2 subunit has demonstrated that in the early embryo, ORC associates with anaphase chromosomes (Baldinger and Gossen, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Clear loading of eGFP-Orc1 onto chromosomes beginning in anaphase was observed, with a 2.7 (±0.4)-fold chromosomal enrichment.
source: Consistent with this observation, we observed clear loading of eGFP-Orc1 onto chromosomes beginning in anaphase, with a 2.7 (±0.4)-fold chromosomal enrichment of eGFP-Orc1 (Figure 5A,C–D and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by lattice light-sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 5A,C-D.

claim: eGFP-Orc1WalkerAB showed wild-type like chromatin association with 2.7 (±0.3)-fold enrichment.
source: Interestingly, eGFP-Orc1WalkerAB also showed wild-type like chromatin association (Figure 5B–D and Figure 5—video 2, 2.7 (±0.3)-fold enrichment).
evidence: The claim is supported by lattice light-sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The initial association of ORC with chromatin in vivo proceeds through a DNA-binding mode that does not require ATP.
source: These data demonstrate that the initial association of ORC with chromatin in vivo proceeds through a DNA-binding mode that does not require ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that Walker mutants associate with chromatin normally.

claim: No significant difference in maximum fold intensity was observed between eGFP-Orc1 and eGFP-Orc1WalkerAB.
source: No difference in maximum fold intensity was observed between eGFP-Orc1 and eGFP-Orc1WalkerAB.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No significant difference was observed between wild-type Orc1, Orc1WalkerAB, and Orc1ΔBAH in telophase chromosome recruitment in S2 cells.
source: No significant difference was observed between WT, Orc1WalkerAB, and Orc1∆BAH, but Orc1∆IDR was not recruited to chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitation shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Orc1ΔIDR was not recruited to chromosomes in S2 cells.
source: No significant difference was observed between WT, Orc1WalkerAB, and Orc1∆BAH, but Orc1∆IDR was not recruited to chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitation shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Chromosome recruitment of Orc1ΔIDR was fully abolished to background levels (1.0 ± 0.2 fold enrichment).
source: By contrast, chromosome recruitment of Orc1ΔIDR was fully abolished to background levels (1.0 ± 0.2 fold enrichment; Figure 5H–I), such that no increase in ORC signal on chromosomes was observed as cells progressed through mitosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitation shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: An Orc1ΔIDR transgene is incapable of rescuing an Orc1 null allele.
source: Finally, we used fly genetics to confirm the essential function of the Orc1 N-terminal IDR, demonstrating that an Orc1ΔIDR transgene is incapable of rescuing an Orc1 null allele (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Table 2.

claim: The Orc1 N-terminal IDR is both essential for viability and facilitates the ATP-independent recruitment of ORC to mitotic chromosomes.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the Orc1 N-terminal IDR is both essential for viability and facilities the ATP-independent recruitment of ORC to mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue and microscopy data.

claim: The association of human and X. laevis ORC with chromatin is regulated by CDK-dependent phosphorylation.
source: Previous work has shown that the association of human and X. laevis ORC with chromatin is regulated by CDK-dependent phosphorylation (Findeisen et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2012; Li et al., 2004; Rowles et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The major sites for CDK action map to the Orc1 IDR.
source: Interestingly, the major sites for CDK action map to the Orc1 IDR and the phosphorylation of these loci interferes with the binding of Drosophila ORC to DNA in vitro (Remus et al., 2005); the binding of D. melanogaster ORC to mitotic chromosomes also requires cessation of CDK activity (Baldinger and Gossen, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Orc1 IDR interferes with the binding of Drosophila ORC to DNA in vitro.
source: Interestingly, the major sites for CDK action map to the Orc1 IDR and the phosphorylation of these loci interferes with the binding of Drosophila ORC to DNA in vitro (Remus et al., 2005); the binding of D. melanogaster ORC to mitotic chromosomes also requires cessation of CDK activity (Baldinger and Gossen, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The binding of D. melanogaster ORC to mitotic chromosomes requires cessation of CDK activity.
source: Interestingly, the major sites for CDK action map to the Orc1 IDR and the phosphorylation of these loci interferes with the binding of Drosophila ORC to DNA in vitro (Remus et al., 2005); the binding of D. melanogaster ORC to mitotic chromosomes also requires cessation of CDK activity (Baldinger and Gossen, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Orc1 hosts sixteen putative CDK phosphorylation sites, all but one of which localizes to the Orc1 IDR.
source: An analysis of putative CDK phosphorylation sites shows that Orc1 hosts sixteen such motifs (Figure 6A), all but one of which localizes to the Orc1 IDR.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Seven Orc1 IDR sites represent full CDK consensus sequences, [S/T]PX[K/R], while the others represent the minimal sequence, [S/T]P.
source: Of these, seven IDR sites represent full CDK consensus sequences, [S/T]PX[K/R], while the others represent the minimal sequence, [S/T]P.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cdc6 has seven putative CDK sites, all residing within the N-terminal IDR, with four representing full consensus sequences.
source: Cdc6 and Cdt1 have seven and sixteen putative sites, respectively. For Cdc6, all sites reside within the N-terminal IDR and four represent full consensus sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cdt1 has sixteen putative CDK sites, with 13/16 sites within the N-terminal IDR and nine representing the full consensus sequence.
source: For Cdt1, 13/16 sites are within the N-terminal IDR and nine represent the full consensus sequence.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Replication initiation factor IDRs retain the vast majority of CDK phosphorylation sites.
source: Thus, replication initiation factor IDRs, which constitute the regions responsible for phase separation, retain the vast majority of CDK phosphorylation sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of CDK sites.

claim: No depletion of ORC is observed when ORC is pre-treated with CDK1/CycA/ATP, but either reagent alone has no effect.
source: No depletion is observed when ORC is pre-treated with CDK1/CycA/ATP, but either reagent alone has no effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Phosphorylated ORC is unable to induce phase separation.
source: Fluorescence microscopy analysis of samples in (C) confirms that phosphorylated ORC is unable to induce phase separation
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ORC phase separation is inhibited by CDK-dependent phosphorylation.
source: Analysis of the reactions by light microscopy corroborated the results of the depletion assay (Figure 6D), demonstrating that ORC phase separation is inhibited by CDK-dependent phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay and microscopy data.

claim: Cdc6 phase separation is inhibited in the presence of both CDK1/CycA and ATP.
source: Although Cdc6 phase separation is inhibited in the presence of both CDK1/CycA and ATP (Figure 6E), it is likewise inhibited by ATP alone and thus a specific effect of phosphorylation could not be assessed.
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Phase separation by Cdt1 was fully inhibited by treatment with CDK1/CycA and ATP, but not by either CDK1/CycA or ATP alone.
source: By comparison, phase separation by Cdt1 was fully inhibited by treatment with CDK1/CycA and ATP, but not by either CDK1/CycA or ATP alone (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by depletion assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: CDK/Cyclin phosphorylation can directly inhibit liquid phase condensation by replication initiation factors.
source: These results demonstrate that CDK/Cyclin phosphorylation can directly inhibit liquid phase condensation by replication initiation factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphorylation and phase separation assays.
